newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian aluminium tolling deals seen safe for now.
newsitem.headline: Russian aluminium tolling deals seen safe for now.

text.p: Russian tax officials denied on Friday local press reports that tolling deals between domestic metal plants and Western trading firms might be phased out completely by April of next year.
Friday's edition of the Sevodnya daily quoted Alexander Pochinok, chairman of the State Tax Service, as saying tolling would be phased out gradually by April 1, 1998.

"The head of the State Tax Service said that by April 1998, tolling schemes (i.e. refining imported raw materials), which have become widespread in the Russian metals industry in the last few years, will be gradually phased out," it quoted Pochinok as saying.
But a spokeswoman for the tax service told Reuters. "I did not hear what Pochinok said, but there is no talk of phasing out such (tolling) schemes by April 1 (1998). This is absolute nonsense."
Senior Russian aluminium officials also played down the report.
"This may be his personal point of view," said Igor Prokopov, general director of the Moscow-based Kontsern Alyuminiy aluminium and alumina producers' group. "It does not mean that this will happen."
Russia's huge aluminium industry is split between those say tolling is crucial to the survival of impoverished plants and those who say plants need greater control over export revenues.

A sudden removal of Western trading firms' rights to operating tolling operations with Russia's giant aluminium smelters could see production and exports of the non-ferrous metal drop sharply, Western analysts said.
Tolling involves Western commodities houses bringing in raw materials for processing and then exporting the ready metal.
Russia is the world's largest exporter of aluminium, used in applications ranging from car parts to drinking cans. Last year, it produced 2.87 million tonnes of aluminium and exported 2.44 million.
Tolling, a multi-billion dollar business, accounts for 60-70 percent of Russian aluminium output.
Cash-strapped aluminium smelters in Siberia have depended on the system for survival during the last six years.

Despite tax officials' denials of plans to end tolling, Russia is considering raising import duties on alumina, making life more expensive for trading companies which currently pay no duty to import raw materials or export finished aluminium.
Trans-World Group of Britain and Swiss-based Glencore AG are the two biggest players in the multi-billion dollar business.
Any hike in costs for the trader would deal a blow to Russian aluminium plants as well, a Trans-World official said.
"Any duty increase will not be good for Trans-World, for other companies similar to Trans-World working in Russia, and for Russian aluminium plants as a whole," the official said from London.
"If the costs of getting alumina to the plants were to rise and we had to pay more for it, then we can't pay the same amount of money in processing fees to the smelters. Everyone pays."
Western analysts said Russian aluminium production could fall if tolling were made unattractive.
The world's two biggest aluminium smelters -- Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk -- are in Siberia, and rely heavily on tolling.
"If the aim of a duty hike was to reduce the level of tolling, then I would expect to see some impact in terms of exports to the West," said one London-based aluminium analyst.
